name: Yeshivish to Plain English Runtime Glossary

entries.yeshivish_example: That was mamesh unbelievable.
entries.plain_english_example: That was truly unbelievable.
entries.context_note: Usually an intensifier meaning “really” or “truly.” In Torah discussion it can also contrast something concrete or literal with something abstract.

entries.yeshivish_example: He's an avreich learning in kollel.
entries.plain_english_example: He's a married Torah scholar studying full-time in a yeshiva.
meanings: married man studying Torah in kollel
entries.context_note: Usually refers to a married Orthodox Jewish man who studies Torah full-time, typically in a kollel. The closest plain-English equivalent depends on context; “full-time Torah scholar” is generally the most natural.

entries.yeshivish_example: He was taka right about the delay.
entries.plain_english_example: He really was right about the delay.
entries.context_note: Often confirms that something is genuinely so. With questioning intonation, it can mean “Really?”

entries.yeshivish_example: Avada we should call them before we come.
entries.plain_english_example: Of course we should call them before we come.
entries.context_note: Used as a confident confirmation, often stronger and more conversational than a plain “yes.”

entries.yeshivish_example: It is pashut that we need more chairs.
entries.plain_english_example: It is obvious that we need more chairs.
entries.context_note: In ordinary conversation it often means “obvious.” In study it can also mean the simple or direct explanation.

entries.yeshivish_example: I was stam asking; I am not upset.
entries.plain_english_example: I was just asking; I am not upset.
entries.context_note: Often softens a statement to mean “just” or “without a special reason.” In textual discussion it can mean an unnamed, unqualified, or default case.

entries.yeshivish_example: Give me a bissel more time.
entries.plain_english_example: Give me a little more time.
entries.context_note: Used for a small quantity or degree and often sounds informal or affectionate.

entries.yeshivish_example: Nu, are we leaving or not?
entries.plain_english_example: Well, are we leaving or not?
entries.context_note: Its meaning depends heavily on tone. It can prompt someone to continue, express impatience, or ask what happens next.

entries.yeshivish_example: Oy vey, I left the keys at home.
entries.plain_english_example: Oh no, I left the keys at home.
entries.context_note: Used for worry, frustration, pain, or dismay. It can be serious or mildly comic depending on tone.

entries.yeshivish_example: You have some shmutz on your shirt.
entries.plain_english_example: You have some dirt on your shirt.
entries.context_note: Usually refers to dirt, grime, or some unwanted dirty substance on a person or object.

entries.yeshivish_example: Gevalt, we are going to miss the train.
entries.plain_english_example: Good grief, we are going to miss the train.
entries.context_note: Traditionally a cry for help, but commonly used as an emphatic reaction to urgency, shock, or exasperation.

entries.yeshivish_example: Nebach, he has been sick all week.
entries.plain_english_example: Unfortunately, he has been sick all week.
entries.context_note: Can express genuine sympathy, but it can also sound pitying or dismissive when applied to a person.

entries.yeshivish_example: I davka wanted the later appointment.
entries.plain_english_example: I specifically wanted the later appointment.
entries.context_note: Marks deliberate or unexpected specificity. Depending on tone, it can mean “specifically,” “precisely,” or “contrary to what you might expect.”

entries.yeshivish_example: Tachlis, what time are we leaving?
entries.plain_english_example: The bottom line is: what time are we leaving?
entries.context_note: Used to move a discussion from theory to the concrete decision, result, or practical point.

entries.yeshivish_example: Yasher koach for organizing the kiddush.
entries.plain_english_example: Thank you for organizing the reception after services.
entries.context_note: Commonly said after someone performs a synagogue honor, teaches, helps, or does something commendable. It combines thanks with praise and encouragement.

entries.yeshivish_example: Mazel tov on your new baby.
entries.plain_english_example: Congratulations on your new baby.
entries.context_note: Said for a birth, engagement, wedding, bar or bat mitzvah, new job, or other happy milestone. It usually means “congratulations,” not ordinary “good luck.”

entries.yeshivish_example: Baruch Hashem, everyone is doing well.
entries.plain_english_example: Thank God, everyone is doing well.
entries.context_note: Used to express gratitude to God, relief, or a positive response to “How are you?”

entries.yeshivish_example: Im yirtzeh Hashem, we will finish tomorrow.
entries.plain_english_example: God willing, we will finish tomorrow.
entries.context_note: Usually attached to a hoped-for future event. It expresses dependence on divine will rather than certainty.

entries.yeshivish_example: B'ezras Hashem, we will open on time.
entries.plain_english_example: With God's help, we will open on time.
entries.context_note: Often used when stating an intention or plan and emphasizing hoped-for divine assistance.

entries.yeshivish_example: Bli neder, I will call you tonight.
entries.plain_english_example: I intend to call you tonight, but I am not making a formal vow.
meanings: I intend to, but not as a formal promise
entries.context_note: Added to a commitment or plan to avoid treating the statement as a binding religious vow. It does not mean the speaker is being casual or insincere.

entries.yeshivish_example: Chas v'shalom, I did not mean that anyone should get hurt.
entries.plain_english_example: God forbid, I did not mean that anyone should get hurt.
entries.context_note: Used to reject or distance an undesirable possibility, accusation, or interpretation.

entries.yeshivish_example: The children are all healthy, kein ayin hara.
entries.plain_english_example: The children are all healthy, and may that good fortune continue.
entries.context_note: Often said after praising health, children, success, or another blessing, reflecting a traditional concern about drawing harmful attention to good fortune.

entries.yeshivish_example: Their house burned down, lo aleinu.
entries.plain_english_example: Their house burned down; may such a tragedy not happen to us.
meanings: may it not happen to us
entries.context_note: Said when mentioning illness, tragedy, or another misfortune, usually as a brief expression of compassion and distance from the calamity.

entries.yeshivish_example: L'maaseh, we only have room for ten people.
entries.plain_english_example: Practically speaking, we only have room for ten people.
entries.context_note: Contrasts the practical conclusion or real situation with theory, appearances, or preliminary discussion.

entries.yeshivish_example: L'choirah, the earlier train is the better choice.
entries.plain_english_example: At first glance, the earlier train is the better choice.
entries.context_note: Introduces a tentative conclusion that may later be questioned or revised.

entries.yeshivish_example: Aderaba, the delay may make the plan easier.
entries.plain_english_example: On the contrary, the delay may make the plan easier.
entries.context_note: Used to reverse the previous assumption and argue that the evidence points the other way.

entries.yeshivish_example: If we call for a small delay, kal vachomer we should call for a full cancellation.
entries.plain_english_example: If we call about a small delay, all the more so we should call about a full cancellation.
entries.context_note: Refers to reasoning from a lighter or less obvious case to a stronger one: if the first is true, the second is even more clearly true.

entries.yeshivish_example: What is the nafka mina between the two plans?
entries.plain_english_example: What practical difference is there between the two plans?
entries.context_note: Asks what changes in practice between two explanations, positions, or facts.

entries.yeshivish_example: My hava amina was that the store closed at six.
entries.plain_english_example: My initial assumption was that the store closed at six.
entries.context_note: In Talmudic discussion, this is a preliminary idea that may be rejected or refined. Conversationally it can mean the assumption someone started with.

entries.yeshivish_example: I have a kashya on that explanation.
entries.plain_english_example: I have a serious question about that explanation.
entries.context_note: Stronger than a request for information. It usually identifies a problem that an explanation or text must resolve.

entries.yeshivish_example: His teretz answers the first problem but not the second.
entries.plain_english_example: His answer resolves the first problem but not the second.
meanings: an explanation that removes a contradiction
entries.context_note: Usually paired conceptually with a kashya: the kashya raises the problem and the teretz resolves it.

entries.yeshivish_example: There is a strong svara for reading the passage that way.
entries.plain_english_example: There is strong reasoning for reading the passage that way.
entries.context_note: Refers to the conceptual logic behind a position, not merely a personal feeling or unsupported opinion.

entries.yeshivish_example: What is the pshat in this sentence?
entries.plain_english_example: What is the straightforward meaning of this sentence?
entries.context_note: Often asks what a text or situation means at the most direct level, before more complex interpretation.

entries.yeshivish_example: The main chiddush of the shiur was the distinction between the two cases.
entries.plain_english_example: The main new insight of the lesson was the distinction between the two cases.
entries.context_note: In study it is an original or newly noticed idea. In conversation it can also refer, sometimes dryly, to something presented as surprising or new.

entries.yeshivish_example: We have a shayla about using the kitchen.
entries.plain_english_example: We have a religious-law question about using the kitchen.
entries.context_note: Can mean any serious question, but often refers to a practical question of Jewish law that should be asked of a rabbi.

entries.yeshivish_example: There is a stira between the two reports.
entries.plain_english_example: There is a contradiction between the two reports.
meanings: a conflict between two statements or facts
entries.context_note: Used when two sources, claims, or observations seem unable to stand together.

entries.yeshivish_example: Let's chazer the material before the test.
entries.plain_english_example: Let's review the material before the test.
entries.context_note: As a verb in yeshiva conversation, it normally means to review learned material. As a Yiddish noun, the same-sounding word can mean a pig, so context is essential.

entries.yeshivish_example: That part of the argument is still shver.
entries.plain_english_example: That part of the argument is still difficult to explain.
entries.context_note: In ordinary speech it means difficult. In learning, it often signals that a text or explanation presents a serious problem.

entries.yeshivish_example: That concern is not shayach in this case.
entries.plain_english_example: That concern is not relevant in this case.
entries.context_note: Usually describes whether a rule, idea, or action belongs in the present case. In some contexts it also means feasible or realistically possible.

entries.yeshivish_example: I am maskim to the revised schedule.
entries.plain_english_example: I agree to the revised schedule.
entries.context_note: Commonly used with English grammar, as in “I am maskim” or “I am maskim to that.”

entries.yeshivish_example: I hear, but I still think the second option is safer.
entries.plain_english_example: I understand your point, but I still think the second option is safer.
entries.context_note: Often acknowledges that the speaker understands an argument without necessarily agreeing with it.

entries.yeshivish_example: What does the Rav hold about this case?
entries.plain_english_example: What position does the rabbi take on this case?
meanings: be at a stage in a process
entries.context_note: The intended meaning depends on its construction. A rabbi can “hold” a legal position; someone may “not hold of” a practice; and “Where are you holding?” can ask how far along someone is.

entries.yeshivish_example: The shiur was really gishmak.
entries.plain_english_example: The lesson was really enjoyable.
entries.context_note: Can describe food, an experience, a lesson, or the pleasure and energy someone feels toward an activity.

entries.yeshivish_example: She is very shtark in her learning.
entries.plain_english_example: She is very serious and committed in her Torah study.
meanings: impressive in religious study or practice
entries.context_note: Often praises someone who learns diligently, prays intensely, or is strongly committed. It can also simply mean physically or conceptually strong.

entries.yeshivish_example: He is a chashuv member of the community.
entries.plain_english_example: He is a highly respected member of the community.
entries.context_note: Usually describes a person, role, institution, or matter that carries genuine standing or significance.

entries.yeshivish_example: He returned the wallet; he is a real mensch.
entries.plain_english_example: He returned the wallet; he is a genuinely decent person.
entries.context_note: More than simply “a person.” Calling someone a mensch praises reliability, consideration, and basic moral character.

entries.yeshivish_example: The children give their grandparents so much nachas.
entries.plain_english_example: The children give their grandparents so much pride and joy.
meanings: satisfaction, especially from children or students
entries.context_note: Usually refers to the deep pleasure someone receives from the good character, growth, or accomplishments of family members or students.

entries.yeshivish_example: He likes to kvetch about the traffic.
entries.plain_english_example: He likes to complain about the traffic.
entries.context_note: Can be a verb or a noun. It usually suggests repeated, fussy, or tiresome complaining rather than a single justified objection.

entries.yeshivish_example: We had to schlep the boxes across town.
entries.plain_english_example: We had to haul the boxes across town.
entries.context_note: As a verb, it emphasizes effort, inconvenience, or reluctance in carrying something or going somewhere. As a noun, “a schlep” is a burdensome trip or task.

entries.yeshivish_example: We stayed after the meeting to schmooze.
entries.plain_english_example: We stayed after the meeting to chat.
entries.context_note: Can be a verb or a noun. It usually means relaxed social conversation and can also imply informal networking; it does not necessarily mean gossip.

entries.yeshivish_example: It took real chutzpah to demand a refund after using the item.
entries.plain_english_example: It took remarkable nerve to demand a refund after using the item.
entries.context_note: Usually criticizes shameless or disrespectful behavior, though tone can sometimes make it admiring when someone shows unusual boldness.

entries.yeshivish_example: The small shul has a very heimish atmosphere.
entries.plain_english_example: The small synagogue has a very warm, familiar atmosphere.
entries.context_note: Can describe a welcoming atmosphere or a style associated with familiar Orthodox or Yiddish-speaking community culture. Its social connotations vary by community.

entries.yeshivish_example: My bubbe is coming for dinner.
entries.plain_english_example: My grandmother is coming for dinner.
meanings: an affectionate name for a grandmother
entries.context_note: Primarily a family term. Some speakers also use it affectionately for an elderly woman, but that can sound overly familiar outside a close relationship.

entries.yeshivish_example: My zaide taught me that song.
entries.plain_english_example: My grandfather taught me that song.
meanings: an affectionate name for a grandfather
entries.context_note: A common Ashkenazi family term for a grandfather.

entries.yeshivish_example: The whole mishpacha is coming for the weekend.
entries.plain_english_example: The whole family is coming for the weekend.
entries.context_note: Can refer to the immediate household or a wider network of relatives. Tone sometimes extends it warmly to people treated like family.

entries.yeshivish_example: The bochur is learning in yeshiva this year.
entries.plain_english_example: The unmarried young man is studying at a yeshiva this year.
entries.context_note: In yeshivish communities it often means an unmarried young man of marriageable age, especially one studying in yeshiva; it does not simply mean any boy.

entries.yeshivish_example: I asked my rebbe to explain the passage again.
entries.plain_english_example: I asked my Jewish studies teacher to explain the passage again.
entries.context_note: In a school or yeshiva, it often means a male Torah teacher. In Hasidic contexts, a Rebbe is the movement's or community's central spiritual leader.

entries.yeshivish_example: I need to ask the rav before we use it.
entries.plain_english_example: I need to ask the rabbi before we use it.
meanings: one's regular rabbi for religious questions
entries.context_note: Often implies a rabbi respected for scholarship or consulted for practical Jewish-law decisions, not merely someone with rabbinic ordination.

entries.yeshivish_example: The rebbetzin is speaking at the program tonight.
entries.plain_english_example: The rabbi's wife is speaking at the program tonight.
meanings: a respected female religious educator or community figure
entries.context_note: Traditionally the title for a rabbi's wife. In some settings it is also used as an honorific for a woman with an independent educational or communal role.

entries.yeshivish_example: Ask the gabbai when the Torah reading begins.
entries.plain_english_example: Ask the synagogue official when the Torah reading begins.
meanings: the person who coordinates services and honors
entries.context_note: In a synagogue, the gabbai commonly organizes prayer logistics, Torah-reading honors, announcements, and related practical matters.

entries.yeshivish_example: The shadchan called with a new suggestion.
entries.plain_english_example: The matchmaker called with a new suggestion.
meanings: someone who proposes or facilitates a marriage match
entries.context_note: May be a professional, a volunteer, a relative, or anyone who suggests and helps manage a potential match.

entries.yeshivish_example: The chosson arrived early for the photographs.
entries.plain_english_example: The groom arrived early for the photographs.
entries.context_note: Can refer to the man at his wedding or, in many communities, throughout the engagement period.

entries.yeshivish_example: The kallah thanked everyone for coming.
entries.plain_english_example: The bride thanked everyone for coming.
entries.context_note: Can refer to the woman at her wedding or throughout the engagement period.

entries.yeshivish_example: They are looking into a shidduch for their daughter.
entries.plain_english_example: They are considering a possible marriage match for their daughter.
meanings: a person considered as a possible spouse
entries.context_note: Usually refers to marriage-oriented dating arranged or suggested through family, friends, or a matchmaker. It does not necessarily mean that the marriage itself is decided in advance.

entries.yeshivish_example: After the third date, he wondered whether she was his bashert.
entries.plain_english_example: After the third date, he wondered whether she was the person he was meant to marry.
entries.context_note: In dating and marriage conversation it often means the person one is destined to marry. It can also describe an event or outcome that feels providentially meant to happen.

entries.yeshivish_example: He shared a short vort at the table.
entries.plain_english_example: He shared a brief Torah thought at the table.
entries.context_note: At a meal or class, a vort is usually a short Torah idea. In some Orthodox communities, “the vort” means a formal engagement gathering or the engagement itself.

entries.yeshivish_example: We are going to a chasunah on Sunday.
entries.plain_english_example: We are going to a wedding on Sunday.
entries.context_note: A common Ashkenazi or Yeshivish word for a wedding, including the ceremony and celebration.

entries.yeshivish_example: The family has a simcha this weekend.
entries.plain_english_example: The family has a happy celebration this weekend.
entries.context_note: In ordinary community conversation, “a simcha” usually means an event such as a wedding, bris, bar mitzvah, or other happy family occasion.

entries.yeshivish_example: The bris will be tomorrow morning.
entries.plain_english_example: The ritual circumcision ceremony will be tomorrow morning.
meanings: the ceremony welcoming a circumcised Jewish baby boy into the covenant
entries.context_note: Usually refers both to the circumcision required by Jewish law and to the ceremony and meal surrounding it.

entries.yeshivish_example: We are going to his bar mitzvah on Sunday.
entries.plain_english_example: We are going to his Jewish coming-of-age celebration on Sunday.
meanings: a Jewish boy who has reached religious adulthood at age thirteen
the ceremony or celebration marking that milestone
entries.context_note: The religious status begins at age thirteen whether or not a party is held. In conversation, “a bar mitzvah” often means the synagogue service, celebration, or both.

entries.yeshivish_example: Her bas mitzvah will be next month.
entries.plain_english_example: Her Jewish coming-of-age celebration will be next month.
meanings: a Jewish girl who has reached religious adulthood at age twelve
the ceremony or celebration marking that milestone
entries.context_note: “Bas mitzvah” is the Ashkenazi or Yeshivish pronunciation; “bat mitzvah” is the common Modern Hebrew form. In Orthodox communities, the form of the celebration varies.

entries.yeshivish_example: There is a kiddush after services.
entries.plain_english_example: There is a reception with refreshments after services.
meanings: the blessing over wine that sanctifies the Sabbath or a festival
refreshments or a reception after synagogue services
entries.context_note: Context determines whether it means the ritual blessing itself or the communal food gathering commonly held after services.

entries.yeshivish_example: He received an aliyah on Shabbos.
entries.plain_english_example: He was called up for the Torah reading on the Sabbath.
meanings: the honor of being called to the Torah during a synagogue service
entries.context_note: In synagogue conversation, someone “gets an aliyah” when called up for the Torah reading or its blessing. Someone who “makes aliyah” moves to Israel.

entries.yeshivish_example: The seudah starts at one o'clock.
entries.plain_english_example: The festive meal starts at one o'clock.
entries.context_note: Often refers to a Sabbath or holiday meal, a wedding meal, or another meal connected to a religious occasion.

entries.yeshivish_example: We should bentsch before everyone leaves.
entries.plain_english_example: We should recite Grace after Meals before everyone leaves.
entries.context_note: In everyday Orthodox speech, it most often means reciting Birkat Hamazon, the formal Grace after Meals, after eating bread. In other phrases it can mean to say a blessing.

entries.yeshivish_example: The cholent needs another hour.
entries.plain_english_example: The slow-cooked Sabbath stew needs another hour.
meanings: a slow-cooked stew traditionally eaten on the Sabbath
entries.context_note: Recipes vary widely, but the term usually means a hot stew prepared before the Sabbath and kept cooking for the daytime meal.

entries.yeshivish_example: This oven is fleishig.
entries.plain_english_example: This oven is designated for meat foods under kosher rules.
meanings: designated for meat under kosher rules
entries.context_note: Can describe food, cookware, a kitchen area, or a person who has recently eaten meat and is waiting before eating dairy.

entries.yeshivish_example: Use the milchig pan for the cheese dish.
entries.plain_english_example: Use the dairy pan for the cheese dish.
meanings: designated for dairy under kosher rules
entries.context_note: Can describe food, cookware, or a kitchen area used for dairy rather than meat.

entries.yeshivish_example: The dessert is pareve, so we can serve it after meat.
entries.plain_english_example: The dessert is neither meat nor dairy, so we can serve it after a meat meal.
meanings: neither meat nor dairy under kosher rules
neutral with respect to meat and dairy
entries.context_note: Pareve food can generally be eaten with either meat or dairy, though preparation equipment and some foods can create additional kosher-law details.

entries.yeshivish_example: Gut Shabbos, everyone.
entries.plain_english_example: Have a good Sabbath, everyone.
entries.context_note: A traditional greeting said before or during the Sabbath, especially from Friday onward. The pronunciation preference determines the generated transliteration.

entries.yeshivish_example: They raised their glasses and said l'chaim.
entries.plain_english_example: They raised their glasses and toasted, “To life.”
meanings: a small celebratory drink or gathering
entries.context_note: Most commonly said as a toast before drinking. It can also refer to the drink or informal gathering itself.

entries.yeshivish_example: We are staying with relatives for Shabbos.
entries.plain_english_example: We are staying with relatives for the Jewish Sabbath.
meanings: the period from Friday before sunset until Saturday night
entries.context_note: The Ashkenazi form “Shabbos” and Modern Hebrew form “Shabbat” refer to the same sacred day. Conversation may use either form for its meals or weekend plans centered on it.

entries.yeshivish_example: The office will be closed for yom tov.
entries.plain_english_example: The office will be closed for the Jewish festival.
meanings: a major Jewish holy day or festival
entries.context_note: Usually refers to a festival or major holy day with special religious observance. The Yiddish forms “yontif” and “yontiff” are common in speech.

entries.yeshivish_example: Erev Shabbos is always busy in our house.
entries.plain_english_example: Friday before the Sabbath is always busy in our house.
meanings: the period of preparation before the Sabbath begins
entries.context_note: Literally the eve of the Sabbath. In ordinary conversation it often means Friday, especially the busy hours devoted to Sabbath preparation.

entries.yeshivish_example: The meeting is motzaei Shabbos.
entries.plain_english_example: The meeting is Saturday night after the Sabbath ends.
meanings: Saturday night after the Sabbath ends
the period immediately following the Sabbath
entries.context_note: Used for scheduling events after nightfall on Saturday, once the Sabbath has concluded.

entries.yeshivish_example: I need to daven Mincha before the meeting.
entries.plain_english_example: I need to pray the afternoon service before the meeting.
meanings: prayer or a prayer service, in the form “davening”
entries.context_note: “Daven” is the verb; “davening” is commonly the activity or service. It usually refers to formal Jewish prayer rather than any informal request to God.

entries.yeshivish_example: We will meet outside the shul.
entries.plain_english_example: We will meet outside the synagogue.
entries.context_note: The everyday Yiddish and Yeshivish word for a synagogue. It may refer to the building, congregation, or local prayer community.

entries.yeshivish_example: There is a minyan at seven.
entries.plain_english_example: There is a communal prayer service at seven.
meanings: a communal prayer group or service
entries.context_note: In Orthodox practice, a minyan is ten adult Jewish males required for certain public prayers. The word also commonly means a particular scheduled service or regular group.

entries.yeshivish_example: Shacharis starts at eight.
entries.plain_english_example: The morning prayer service starts at eight.
entries.context_note: The Ashkenazi form “shacharis” and the Israeli or Sephardi form “shacharit” refer to the same daily morning service.

entries.yeshivish_example: We can daven mincha before dinner.
entries.plain_english_example: We can pray the afternoon service before dinner.
entries.context_note: Usually refers to the daily afternoon service. The exact time varies with the day and local schedule.

entries.yeshivish_example: Maariv begins ten minutes after sunset.
entries.plain_english_example: The evening prayer service begins ten minutes after sunset.
entries.context_note: The common Ashkenazi name for the evening service; many Sephardi and Israeli speakers call it Arvit.

entries.yeshivish_example: We learned that gemara last week.
entries.plain_english_example: We studied that Talmudic passage last week.
meanings: the Talmudic discussion surrounding the Mishnah
a volume or passage of Talmud being studied
entries.context_note: In yeshiva conversation, “Gemara” often means the Babylonian Talmud generally, a particular tractate, or the passage currently under discussion.

entries.yeshivish_example: The shiur begins at nine.
entries.plain_english_example: The Torah class begins at nine.
meanings: a prescribed measurement or minimum quantity in Jewish law
entries.context_note: In ordinary scheduling, it usually means a class. In legal discussion, it can mean a defined amount, size, or measure.

entries.yeshivish_example: My chavrusa is away this week.
entries.plain_english_example: My study partner is away this week.
entries.context_note: Can refer to either the person one studies with or the regular period of paired textual study.

entries.yeshivish_example: He is waiting in the beis midrash.
entries.plain_english_example: He is waiting in the Torah study hall.
meanings: a room or building used for Torah study, often also for prayer
entries.context_note: Usually the central study space of a yeshiva or synagogue. It may function as both a learning hall and a prayer room.

entries.yeshivish_example: He plans to attend yeshiva next year.
entries.plain_english_example: He plans to attend a Jewish school focused on Torah study next year.
meanings: a Jewish school centered on Torah study
an academy for advanced Talmud study
entries.context_note: The word covers different age levels and institutions, but in Yeshivish speech it often evokes intensive traditional Torah and Talmud study.

entries.yeshivish_example: He learns in the kollel every morning.
entries.plain_english_example: He studies Torah in the advanced program every morning.
meanings: a framework in which married men study Torah full time or extensively
entries.context_note: Most often refers to a post-yeshiva institution or program for married scholars, though structures and schedules differ.

entries.yeshivish_example: First seder starts at nine.
entries.plain_english_example: The first scheduled study period starts at nine.
entries.context_note: In a yeshiva schedule, “seder” means a formal block of study. In holiday conversation, “the Seder” usually means the Passover meal and ritual.

entries.yeshivish_example: He is teaching a new class this zman.
entries.plain_english_example: He is teaching a new class this academic term.
entries.context_note: When someone says “this zman” or “next zman,” the usual Yeshivish meaning is an academic term in the yeshiva calendar.

entries.yeshivish_example: They are traveling during bein hazmanim.
entries.plain_english_example: They are traveling during the break between yeshiva terms.
entries.context_note: Literally “between the times.” It is the interval between formal yeshiva study terms, when regular schedules are reduced or suspended.

entries.yeshivish_example: The rosh yeshiva will speak after Maariv.
entries.plain_english_example: The head of the yeshiva will speak after the evening service.
meanings: senior Torah scholar and educational leader of a yeshiva
entries.context_note: Usually denotes the institution's leading scholarly authority, not merely an administrative principal.

entries.yeshivish_example: He is in learning full time.
entries.plain_english_example: He studies Torah full time.
meanings: the activity or career of intensive religious study
entries.context_note: In Yeshivish, “learning” often specifically means studying Torah or Talmud, not education in general. “In learning” can describe someone devoted to full-time or sustained Torah study.

entries.yeshivish_example: Can you bring down the source for that ruling?
entries.plain_english_example: Can you cite the source for that ruling?
meanings: record a teaching in a text
entries.context_note: A source, book, or speaker can “bring down” an earlier opinion or teaching. It normally means cite or transmit, not physically lower something.

entries.yeshivish_example: What is the halacha in this situation?
entries.plain_english_example: What does Jewish law require in this situation?
meanings: a specific legal ruling or rule
entries.context_note: Can refer to the overall system of Jewish law or to one particular rule. In conversation, “What is the halacha?” asks what Jewish law requires in a specific case.

entries.yeshivish_example: Visiting the sick is a mitzvah.
entries.plain_english_example: Visiting the sick is a religiously significant good deed.
entries.context_note: Its primary meaning is a commandment or commanded act. In casual English it can mean a good deed, but in Orthodox speech the connection to religious obligation remains important.

entries.yeshivish_example: He realized that taking it would be an aveirah.
entries.plain_english_example: He realized that taking it would be a religious transgression.
entries.context_note: Refers to doing something prohibited or failing a religious duty, with seriousness depending on the specific act and circumstances.

entries.yeshivish_example: Is this restaurant kosher?
entries.plain_english_example: Does this restaurant follow Jewish dietary law?
meanings: prepared or supervised according to kosher rules
entries.context_note: Most often describes food, ingredients, utensils, or facilities that meet Jewish dietary requirements. Figuratively, it can mean acceptable or aboveboard.

entries.yeshivish_example: That meat is treif.
entries.plain_english_example: That meat is not kosher.
meanings: forbidden as food under Jewish dietary law
entries.context_note: Usually describes food or food equipment that is not kosher. Informally it can also label an idea or situation as religiously unacceptable.

entries.yeshivish_example: Which hechsher is on this package?
entries.plain_english_example: Which kosher certification is on this package?
entries.context_note: On food, it usually means the certification or symbol showing rabbinic kosher supervision. In broader discussion it can mean formal approval or validation.

entries.yeshivish_example: It is assur to use that ingredient.
entries.plain_english_example: Jewish law forbids using that ingredient.
entries.context_note: A legal classification, not merely a personal preference or community custom. The reason and severity depend on the issue.

entries.yeshivish_example: The rav said it is mutar in this case.
entries.plain_english_example: The rabbi said it is permitted in this case.
entries.context_note: Means that Jewish law permits the act; it does not necessarily mean the act is recommended or ideal.

entries.yeshivish_example: L'chatchila, use a separate utensil.
entries.plain_english_example: Ideally, use a separate utensil.
entries.context_note: Describes what should be done before the fact when one can choose the best procedure, as distinct from what may still count afterward.

entries.yeshivish_example: B'dieved, the meal can still be served.
entries.plain_english_example: After the fact, the meal can still be served.
entries.context_note: Used when an action was not performed in the preferred way but may still be accepted after it happened.

entries.yeshivish_example: Can I be yotzei with this bracha?
entries.plain_english_example: Can I fulfill the obligation with this blessing?
entries.context_note: Commonly asks whether a particular action, blessing, or performance counts as fulfilling the required mitzvah.

entries.yeshivish_example: They moved to a neighborhood with a large frum community.
entries.plain_english_example: They moved to a neighborhood with a large Orthodox observant community.
entries.context_note: Usually describes a person, family, institution, or environment committed to Orthodox observance. Exact standards and social connotations vary by speaker.

entries.yeshivish_example: He became a baal teshuvah in college.
entries.plain_english_example: He became religiously observant in college after a less-observant upbringing.
meanings: a person who became religiously observant later in life
a person who returned to Jewish observance
entries.context_note: Usually describes a Jew raised with less Orthodox observance who later adopted an observant life. It does not mean a convert to Judaism.

entries.yeshivish_example: He went off the derech in his late teens.
entries.plain_english_example: He stopped living an Orthodox observant life in his late teens.
meanings: no longer following the Orthodox religious path
having left or substantially reduced observance after an Orthodox upbringing
entries.context_note: A sensitive community label, often used for someone raised Orthodox who no longer observes that way. It can oversimplify a person's identity and should be used carefully.

entries.yeshivish_example: The job is suitable for someone who is shomer Shabbos.
entries.plain_english_example: The job is suitable for someone who observes the Jewish Sabbath.
meanings: a person who follows the laws of the Sabbath
entries.context_note: Literally “one who keeps the Sabbath.” In many Orthodox settings it may suggest broader observance as well, but its direct meaning concerns the Sabbath.

entries.yeshivish_example: We should not repeat that; it may be loshon hara.
entries.plain_english_example: We should not repeat that; it may be prohibited harmful gossip.
meanings: prohibited harmful speech about another person
entries.context_note: In Jewish law, the term can include harmful negative information even when it is true; false damaging speech is treated under related but distinct rules. Context and permitted purposes matter.

entries.yeshivish_example: Finding the document just then felt like hashgacha pratis.
entries.plain_english_example: Finding the document just then felt like an instance of individual divine providence.
entries.context_note: Often used when an event, coincidence, or outcome is understood as personally guided by God rather than merely accidental.

entries.yeshivish_example: We can nosh on something before we leave.
entries.plain_english_example: We can have a snack before we leave.
meanings: to eat something casually or in small amounts
a snack or tasty bite to eat
entries.context_note: Used as both a verb and a noun. As a verb, it usually means to snack or eat something casually rather than sit down for a full meal. As a noun, a nosh is a snack or small amount of tasty food.

entries.yeshivish_example: He is looking for steady parnassa.
entries.plain_english_example: He is looking for a steady livelihood.
meanings: the means of supporting a household
entries.context_note: Can refer to a job, earnings, or the broader need for financial sustenance, often with an implicit religious sense that livelihood is a blessing.

entries.yeshivish_example: They set aside part of every paycheck for tzedakah.
entries.plain_english_example: They set aside part of every paycheck for charitable giving.
meanings: money or aid given to people in need
a religious duty of material support
entries.context_note: Usually translated as charity, but it carries a stronger sense of obligation and justice than purely optional generosity.

entries.yeshivish_example: We borrowed a folding table from the gemach.
entries.plain_english_example: We borrowed a folding table from the community lending service.
meanings: an organization that lends money or useful items without charge
entries.context_note: Originally associated with interest-free loans, but a gemach may lend medical equipment, clothing, household items, or other resources.

entries.yeshivish_example: He is machmir about that certification.
entries.plain_english_example: He follows a stricter religious-law standard for that certification.
meanings: strict or stringent in Jewish-law practice
following a more demanding accepted position
entries.context_note: Describes a person, ruling, or choice that adopts a stricter halachic standard. It should not automatically be translated as more religious or more correct.

entries.yeshivish_example: This rabbi is meikil in that specific case.
entries.plain_english_example: This rabbi follows a more lenient accepted ruling in that specific case.
meanings: following a less restrictive accepted position
entries.context_note: Describes a legitimate lenient ruling or practice within Jewish law; it does not necessarily imply carelessness.

entries.yeshivish_example: Bringing meals to the family was a real chesed.
entries.plain_english_example: Bringing meals to the family was a genuine act of kindness.
entries.context_note: Can mean a single helpful act or an ongoing commitment to caring for others, often through meals, visits, rides, loans, or communal support.

entries.yeshivish_example: Which bracha do we say on this food?
entries.plain_english_example: Which blessing do we recite over this food?
meanings: a wish for well-being or success
entries.context_note: Can refer to a formal blessing recited before food or a mitzvah, a personal blessing from a respected person, or a general expression of good wishes.
The context determines whether the emphasis is moral repentance or renewed religious observance.
Usually expresses admiration for a woman's character or religious devotion.
